item.title: Depth-adaptive calibration of line-laser 3D measurement systems using rational polynomial mapping and depth-independent misalignment compensation
item.description:
The problem

A line-laser profiler measures a surface by triangulation. A camera watches the laser stripe on the object and converts each stripe pixel (u, v) into physical coordinates (X, Z) in the laser plane. A full 3D point cloud is then built by stitching many such profiles while a motion stage scans the part. Measurement accuracy is therefore set by calibration, and two different errors erode it across the working depth of field.

The first error is internal. Conventional calibration rests on a single-plane homography, a strictly linear pixel-to-physical mapping. In a real system, slight tilt of the lifting stage, local non-flatness of the target, radial and tangential lens distortion and stripe-centre extraction noise push the observations away from that ideal perspective, and a pure homography cannot represent the non-linear deviation. The second error is external. If the sensor is not aligned with the motion axis, the stitched cloud carries a systematic shear, and an orthogonal rectangle comes out as a parallelogram. Tuning intrinsics or distortion coefficients cannot remove this shear, and correcting each depth with its own parameters multiplies the parameter count. Existing pipelines usually address either the internal mapping or the external installation geometry, and their joint effect across the depth of field is seldom modelled.

How it works

The method handles the two errors in two separate stages. The internal stage is a one-off factory calibration that fixes the pixel-to-physical mapping inside each profile. The external stage is an on-site compensation that removes the installation shear from the stitched cloud. An automated, motion-triggered workflow runs both, so no manual multi-pose target placement is needed.

  1. Sample the full depth range. The camera and line laser are mounted on a precision Z-axis stage that moves through programmed positions. At each height the system captures a laser-on/laser-off image pair, which yields a clean stripe centreline. In the experiments, six depths Z1–Z6 are spaced 30 mm apart over a 150 mm range. Five are used for fitting, and Z3 is held out for testing.
  2. Fit one rational polynomial mapping. The model keeps the perspective (homography) backbone and adds a bivariate cubic residual in the height direction. Merged into one ratio, it maps (u, v) to X and to Z with a cubic numerator over a shared linear denominator, 22 coefficients in total. Cross-multiplying makes the problem linear, and the correspondences from all training depths form one overdetermined system, solved by least squares.
  3. Model the shear. The installation error is split into three rotations: roll α, pitch β and yaw γ. With a yaw angle γ, a scan step Δy pushes points sideways by Δx = Δy tan γ, so a rectangle turns into a parallelogram. In the tested push-broom setup, pitch rotates the laser plane about its own axial direction and causes no in-plane shear, so β is set to zero.
  4. Measure α and γ. A RANSAC line fit to a scan of the empty platform gives a reference line L. Roll comes from a standard height block of nominal height H and width W: α = arctan((H′ − H) / W), where H′ is the measured mean height of its upper face above L. Yaw comes from a checkerboard: requiring adjacent edges of a corrected cell to be perpendicular gives a quadratic equation in sin γ. It is solved for every interior 2 × 2 corner cell, and the median is used.
  5. Undo the rotation, once for all depths. Every point is mapped through the inverse rotation in Z–Y–X order, Rx(α) Ry(β) Rz(γ), which reduces to Rx(α) Rz(γ) with β = 0. The correction does not depend on depth, so angles estimated once at Z3 are reused across the whole volume.

Results

Mean absolute error 17.5% lower in X and 11.8% lower in Z than the HALCON calibration baseline on the held-out depth Z3: 8.745 vs 10.600 µm and 3.820 vs 4.332 µm (Table 5).
Error in the measured angle of a 25° standard block, tilted installation: 0.7591° → 0.0387° (deviation from 25°), depth-mean, a 94.90% reduction (Table 7).
Checkerboard orthogonality error, tilted installation: 10.007° → 0.309° (deviation of adjacent edges from perpendicular), depth-mean, a 96.92% reduction (Table 8).

All experiments use one commercial line-laser profiler (OPT-LPF2-006-01) on a programmable Z-stage and a push-broom rig. Ground truth comes from certified standards: a grid distortion target with a 49 × 49 dot array at 1 mm pitch, a metal checkerboard with 25 mm cells, a 25° standard angle block and a height block. For the internal stage, the HALCON baseline and the proposed mapping used the same image stack, the same stripe-centre extractor and the same train/test depth split. Besides the lower mean absolute errors, the proposed mapping improved repeatability by 33.8% in X and 70.0% in Z. The largest gain is in Z repeatability, the metric most sensitive to height-direction nonlinearity, which the cubic residual is designed to absorb.

A sweep over the residual order supports the cubic choice: a quadratic residual underfits, and a quartic one reaches the lowest training error, but its held-out error rises to 12.155 µm in X and 5.130 µm in Z, against 8.745 and 3.820 µm for the cubic residual (Table 11).

For the external stage, the sensor was deliberately tilted (roll α ≈ 5°, yaw γ ≈ 10°) and measured at all six depths in three states: normal installation, tilted without compensation, and tilted with compensation, with 10 trials each. Compared with normal installation, the tilt raised the angle-block error by a factor of 18.84 and the orthogonality error by a factor of 31.87. With the angles frozen from Z3, compensation brought both back to the level of normal installation (0.96× and 0.98× of it). The per-depth reduction stayed within 94.69%–95.04% for the angle and 96.87%–96.97% for orthogonality, so one compensator handles every depth without retuning.

Both stages are needed. With the external compensator disabled, the mapping errors match the full pipeline, but the angle and orthogonality errors stay at their uncompensated levels. With HALCON’s mapping plus the external compensator, the geometric errors drop to 0.0506° and 0.519°, but stay above the full pipeline’s 0.0387° and 0.309°, and the mapping errors return to the baseline (Table 10). The compensator also kept working beyond the vendor’s nominal 5° mounting tolerance: at Z3, with roll swept up to 20° at a yaw of about 10°, the corrected angle error stayed within 0.037°–0.101° and the orthogonality error within 0.16°–0.59° (Table 9). The numerical part of a full calibration takes about 2.3 s, and the total of about 11 minutes is dominated by physical scanning (Table 12).

The authors scope these results to the single tested device and working-distance range. Validation on a second camera, additional standard angles and the repeatability of the estimated angles across independent re-mountings are left to future work.

item.title: TTA-MAC: Per-Instance Test-Time CAD-Anchored Refinement of Monocular Depth Calibration and 6D Object Pose
item.description:
The problem

Zero-shot 6D object pose from a single RGB image has advanced quickly thanks to foundation detectors and monocular depth models. A central bottleneck remains, according to the authors: metric grounding. Monocular depth gives rich relative geometry, but its scale and shift are biased for each object instance. A global CAD-guided affine calibration such as CAD-MAC reduces this bias, yet the remaining residual can be strongly non-Gaussian: on LineMod-Occlusion with the DAv2 depth model, its skewness is +4.5 and its excess kurtosis +36. A Gaussian prior for per-instance refinement therefore fits the actual errors poorly.

How it works

TTA-MAC is a CAD-anchored refinement layer applied at test time. It takes a frozen detector, a frozen monocular depth backbone, a warm-start pose and the object’s CAD model, and refines only eight geometric variables: the two calibration scalars of the monocular depth and the 6D pose.

  • Per-instance MAP problem. The depth-derived point cloud is aligned to a signed distance field computed from the CAD model.
  • Heavy-tailed prior. A Student-t prior models the heavy-tailed calibration residuals.
  • Trust region. The refinement runs inside a trust region with three gates and restores the best state found so far. The key safeguard is a signed-SDF gate on the fraction of the pseudo-depth cloud that lies inside the CAD volume. This detects wrong-basin states where the cloud penetrates the object, a failure that ordinary ICP or unsigned-distance alignment cannot see.

Results

Compared with a CAD-MAC+ICP baseline, the median ADD error improves from 44.0 mm to 31.3 mm on LineMod-Occlusion, and the success rate (ADD below 10% of the object diameter) rises from 10.4% to 14.3%. On LineMOD, across 18,273 instances, the median ADD improves from 43.5 mm to 30.5 mm and the success rate from 17.3% to 23.3%. The transfer to other datasets is partial: the median ADD improves from 41.1 mm to 38.3 mm on YCB-V and from 59.5 mm to 55.6 mm on TUD-L, and these runs also expose remaining threshold and over-refinement failures. The authors name visibility-aware, symmetry-aware and occlusion-robust trust regions as future directions.

This page summarises the abstract of the manuscript; details will be added once the paper is published.

item.title: Calibration Method of Fringe Projection Based on High-Order Polynomial
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) measures 3D shape by projecting sinusoidal fringes onto an object, recovering the phase of the deformed fringes in the camera image, and converting pixel coordinates and phase into 3D coordinates. That conversion is set by system calibration, and the traditional approaches are laborious. Phase-to-height mapping needs a large, precise calibration target and a precision translation stage, and its parameters depend on how accurately both are made and moved. Stereo-vision calibration takes the target coordinates and their image coordinates in the camera and the projector, and solves for the parameters by nonlinear optimisation. That is slow, and the accuracy depends on how well those image coordinates are measured.

A polynomial calibration model avoids the projector model and the translation stage: it directly fits the 3D world coordinates as a polynomial in the pixel coordinates (u, v) and the absolute phase ϕ. Higher orders describe this relationship more accurately, but the number of coefficients grows quickly, and fitting them by least squares becomes slow and unstable once the order exceeds 3. An earlier simplification removes redundant terms by principal component analysis, which speeds the fit up but lowers reconstruction accuracy.

How it works

The method keeps a high-order polynomial calibration model, which needs no projector model and no translation stage, and replaces least-squares fitting with a sparse greedy randomized Kaczmarz (SGRK) solver. SGRK combines the efficient iterations of the randomized sparse Kaczmarz method with the selection strategy of greedy algorithms: each step works on one well-chosen equation instead of the whole system.

  1. Collect calibration points. Fringes are projected onto a circle-grid board placed in several poses. The circle centres are the feature points: each gives its pixel coordinates (u, v), its absolute phase ϕ from three-frequency four-step phase shifting, and its world coordinates from Zhang’s calibration method.
  2. Set up the polynomial model. Each world coordinate X, Y and Z is written as an n-th order polynomial in u, v and ϕ, so calibration becomes a linear system W = Ax. The model has 60 coefficients at order 3, 105 at order 4 and 168 at order 5; the paper uses order 4 as its standard model, balancing accuracy and computing time.
  3. Choose an equation greedily. In each iteration SGRK computes the residual of every equation, keeps the rows whose residual exceeds a threshold, and draws one of them with probability proportional to its squared residual. Equations with large errors are therefore updated first, which speeds up convergence.
  4. Update and sparsify. The chosen row updates the coefficients by a weighted Kaczmarz projection, and a soft-threshold operation then sets small coefficients to zero, so the solution stays sparse.
  5. Iterate, then reconstruct. The loop runs until the relative standard error (RSE) of the coefficients falls below 10⁻⁶. To measure an object, the pixel coordinates and absolute phase of each point are put into the fitted polynomial to give its 3D coordinates.

Results

Standard ceramic sphere (25.0001 mm), 4th-order model: diameter deviation 0.0232 mm in 1.63 s with SGRK, against 0.0727 mm in 3.96 s with least squares (Table 2).
Standard step block, 4th-order model: average errors of 0.004 and −0.003 mm on the two step heights in 1.78 s, against 0.009 and 0.006 mm in 4.32 s with least squares (Table 1).
Ceramic doll: RMSE 0.0729 mm with SGRK versus 0.9250 mm with least squares, measured against a Mech-Eye Pro S Enhanced scan (Sec. 3, Fig. 9).

The system uses a DLP LightCrafter 4500 projector (912 × 1140 pixels), a CCD camera (1280 × 1024 pixels) and a 300 mm × 300 mm circle board with 30 mm between circle centres. Each method was compared on the full 4th-order model and on the PCA-simplified 4th-order model. SGRK was faster and more accurate in both cases: on the sphere the simplified model gave 0.0449 mm in 1.17 s with SGRK against 0.0932 mm in 3.17 s with least squares, and the simplified models were less accurate than the full one for both solvers (Table 2). The step block was measured three times after each calibration to check repeatability (Table 1).

The advantage holds at other orders too (Table 3). At order 3, SGRK gave a sphere diameter deviation of 0.0549 mm in 1.02 s against 0.1470 mm in 3.04 s for least squares; at order 5, 0.0177 mm in 2.31 s against 0.0400 mm in 6.15 s. The 5th-order model is more accurate than the 4th, but its 168 coefficients make the computation markedly longer, and both are more accurate than the 3rd-order model.
